problems.cpp_vs_py:

=====================================================================
cpp_alts: `static const string KEYS[10]` indexed by `digits[i] - '0'` beats a map.
`string path` with `push_back`/`pop_back` avoids the $O(n)$ copy that `path + ch` forces at every node.
py_alts: Mutate a single list with append/pop instead of concatenating strings -- avoids an $O(L)$ copy per node.
A dict keyed by digit character is clearer than a list indexed by digit minus zero.
problems.trap: Indexing the keys table with the digit's character value rather than the digit minus '0'. That reads out of bounds and returns the wrong key for every multi-digit input.
problems.invariant: `dfs(i, path)` enumerates all completions of the suffix starting at digit index i. The recursion is exhaustive because every letter of digit i is tried, and it emits no duplicates because each output corresponds to exactly one choice sequence.

questions.q: What is the size of the output space?
questions.a: The product of the letter counts, between $2^n$ and $4^n$. For n = 8 that is up to 65536 combinations, so any solution is output-bound: the algorithm is $\Theta(\text{output size})$ and cannot beat enumeration.

questions.q: Why not a greedy per-position choice?
questions.a: Every letter at every position is valid independently -- there is no constraint linking positions. So the solution set is the cartesian product, which is exactly what recursion over independent choices generates.

questions.q: How does string concatenation affect the complexity?
questions.a: `path + ch` copies the whole prefix each time, making the traversal $\Theta(n \cdot \text{output})$ in the worst case. Mutating one buffer with push/pop brings it down to $\Theta(\text{output})$, which is optimal.

problems.core_objective: Return all combinations that sum to target, where each number may be used unlimited times.
problems.bounds: 1 <= candidates.length <= 30 and 1 <= target <= 30, so the output is small but recursion depth is bounded by target (each element adds at least 1). Zero targets would loop forever.

approaches.aha: dfs(i, rem): rem == 0 → record. For j in i..n: skip c[j] > rem (prune), take, recurse(j) — same j = unlimited use — then pop.
approaches.why: Follows directly from the traversal count: ? time, ? space.

approaches.aha: dp[t] lists combos for sum t; extend dp[t-c] with c for t = c..T. --------------------------------------------------------------------- DEEP DIVE · The one-character difference from Subsets II recurse(j+1) forbids reuse; recurse(j) allows it. problems.cpp_vs_py:
recurse(j+1) forbids reuse; recurse(j) allows it. The j from the LOOP start also forbids order permutations (no (2,3) after (3,2)) because j only moves forward. Pruning c[j] > rem cuts most of the tree when the target is small relative to candidates. --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(n^(target/min)) worst case.

=====================================================================
cpp_alts: Sort candidates and prune with `if (c[i] > rem) break` -- a large practical speedup.
Pass `vector<int>& cur` by reference and push/pop, avoiding a copy per leaf.
py_alts: Sorting the list first and breaking out of the loop early prunes an enormous amount of the tree.
`cur + [c]` at the leaf copies once per solution, which is acceptable since it happens only at output points.
problems.trap: Recursing with `i + 1` instead of `i`, which silently forbids reuse and returns only [[7]] for the example above. The distinction between problems 39 and 40 is exactly one character.
problems.invariant: `dfs(i, rem)` enumerates all combinations summing to `rem` drawn from candidates[i:]. Recursing with the same `i` permits unbounded reuse of candidates[i], and recursing with `i+1` guarantees combinations are generated in non-decreasing candidate order, so no solution is produced twice.

questions.q: Why does starting at the same index prevent duplicates?
questions.a: Because a combination like [2,3] can only be built by taking 2 then 3. If you always move forward or stay, you never build [3,2], and the monotonic construction is unique per multiset. Sorting makes this even more obvious by letting you break when a candidate exceeds the remainder.

questions.q: What bounds the recursion depth?
questions.a: The target, since each element is at least 1 -- depth is at most `target`. With candidates containing 0 the recursion would not terminate, so a zero candidate requires an explicit guard.

questions.q: How do you prune aggressively?
questions.a: Sort ascending, then at each level break as soon as candidates[i] > rem. Any later candidate is larger, so the entire remaining subtree at that level is infeasible. This typically removes most of the tree.

problems.one_liner: Same index, but start at i+1 and skip duplicate values.
problems.core_objective: Return all unique combinations that sum to target, using each input element at most once.
problems.bounds: 1 <= candidates.length <= 30, all values 1..30, distinct, target 1..40. Duplicates in the input must produce duplicate combinations, so input-level dedupe is mandatory.

approaches.name: · Sorted DFS (best)
approaches.aha: for j in i..n: if j > i and c[j]==c[j-1]: continue; if c[j] > rem: break; take, recurse(j+1), pop.
approaches.why: the sort dominates; the post-sort scan is linear; hence the stated bounds.

approaches.name: · Frequency-map branching
approaches.aha: Group values with counts; branch per distinct value 0..cnt copies. --------------------------------------------------------------------- DEEP DIVE · break vs continue after sorting In Combination Sum I (unlimited use, unsorted) we `continue` because a big candidate doesn't rule out smaller ones later. Here sorting guarantees c[j] > rem ⇒ every later candidate is also too big, so `break` prunes harder with identical semantics. --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(2^n) worst case. MEMORY COMPLEXITY: O(n). =====================================================================

problems.diagram:
candidates = [10,1,2,7,6,1,5], target = 8

  KEY: dedupe the INPUT first -> [1,1,2,5,6,7,10]
  at each level: skip i > 0 and candidates[i]==candidates[i-1]

  dfs(i=0, rem=8), path=[]:
    i=0 c=1 -> dfs(1, 7)
      i=1 c=1 == c[0] -> SKIP (same value as previous)
      i=2 c=2 -> dfs(3, 5)
        i=3 c=5 -> dfs(4, 0) HIT [1,2,5]
        i=4 c=6 > 5 break
      i=3 c=5 -> dfs(4, 2) 6>2 break
    i=1 c=1 == c[0] -> SKIP
    i=2 c=2 -> ...
    i=3 c=5 -> ...
    i=5 c=7 -> dfs(6, 1) 10>1 break
    i=6 c=10 > 8 break

  the two skips:
   i > 0 and c[i] == c[i-1]  -> skip duplicates AT a level
   recurse with i + 1          -> element used at most once
problems.cpp_vs_py:
In Combination Sum I (unlimited use, unsorted) we `continue` because a big candidate doesn't rule out smaller ones later. Here sorting guarantees c[j] > rem ⇒ every later candidate is also too big, so `break` prunes harder with identical semantics. --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(2^n) worst case.

=====================================================================
cpp_alts: Sort then dedupe the vector in place before searching -- makes the per-level skip correct.
`break` when `c[i] > rem` after sorting removes whole subtrees.
py_alts: `cands = sorted(set(candidates))` does dedupe and sort in one step, which is both correct and faster than a manual pass.
`i > 0 and cands[i] == cands[i-1]` is the canonical skip; using `i == start` is a common wrong variant.
problems.trap: Skipping with `i == start` instead of `i > 0`. That check compares against the position where the current combination began, not against the previous element, so duplicate values in the input still generate duplicate combinations.
problems.invariant: With the input sorted and deduped and the rule "skip c[i] if it equals c[i-1] and i > 0", every multiset of candidates has exactly one representation: the increasing-index selection of its distinct positions. Combined with recursing at i+1, no element is reused and no combination repeats.

questions.q: Why must the input be sorted before the per-level skip works?
questions.a: The skip compares adjacent elements, which only detects duplicates if equal values are adjacent. Sorting guarantees that, and it also enables the `c[i] > rem` early break. Sorting first is a precondition, not an optimisation.

questions.q: What is the difference from problem 39 exactly?
questions.a: Two changes: recurse with `i + 1` (single use) instead of `i` (reuse), and add the duplicate skip. Applying only the first to problem 39's repeated candidates would lose valid solutions; applying only the second leaves 39 unable to express repeats.

questions.q: Can you solve it without sorting?
questions.a: Yes, using a `Counter` over candidates and choosing values in a fixed order with a count limit -- that also avoids duplicates structurally. It costs a hash map instead of a sort but has the same $O(n \log n)$-ish bound after sorting.

problems.one_liner: One position at a time, choosing any unused value.
problems.core_objective: Return all permutations of a collection of distinct integers.
problems.bounds: 1 <= nums.length <= 6, so at most 720 permutations -- output-bound, and every approach is fast. Values are distinct, so a bitmap suffices; duplicates would need a set.

approaches.name: · Swap-based DFS (best)
approaches.aha: dfs(pos): pos == n → record. For j in pos..n-1: swap(pos,j), recurse, swap back.
approaches.py:
out = []
n = len(nums)
    if pos == n:
        out.append(nums[:])
        return
    for j in range(pos, n):
        nums[pos], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[pos]
        dfs(pos + 1)
approaches.why: every node is visited once and returns O(1) state; hence the stated bounds.

approaches.name: · used[] bitmap + running permutation
approaches.aha: Mark used[i], append nums[i], recurse, pop + unmark. --------------------------------------------------------------------- DEEP DIVE · Two state encodings, one search tree Swap version: after fixing position pos the elements left of pos are exactly the used ones — state lives in the array (zero extra memory, no copies). used[] version copies the permutation at each leaf but is easier to read. Both enumerate n! leaves. --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(n · n!) MEMORY COMPLEXITY: O(n). =====================================================================

        path=[1,3,2] -> EMIT [1,3,2]
    path=[1,3]
      path=[1,3,2] -> EMIT [1,3,2]  (dup? no, different prefix)
      path=[1,3,1]? -> 1 already used, skipped

problems.cpp_vs_py:
Swap version: after fixing position pos the elements left of pos are exactly the used ones — state lives in the array (zero extra memory, no copies). used[] version copies the permutation at each leaf but is easier to read. Both enumerate n! leaves. --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(n · n!)

=====================================================================
cpp_alts: `next_permutation` from `<algorithm>` generates all permutations iteratively in $O(n \cdot n!)$ with $O(1)$ extra space.
The swap-based DFS (`do { emit } while (next_permutation(...))`) is usually the strongest C++ answer.
py_alts: `itertools.permutations(nums)` is a C-level lazy iterator -- the shortest and fastest answer.
A `used` boolean list is faster than swapping or a set when values are distinct ints.
problems.trap: Emitting a copy of `path` at every node instead of only at depth n. That produces partial permutations too, and the count is wrong by a large factor.
problems.invariant: `path` contains distinct values all drawn from nums, and `used` marks exactly the positions represented in it. Appending an unused value preserves distinctness, so every depth-n path is a valid permutation, and every permutation is reachable by appending its elements in order.

questions.q: Why is every permutation generated exactly once?
questions.a: Each permutation corresponds to exactly one ordering of choices, and the recursion tries each unused element at each level. Two different choice sequences produce different paths, so no permutation can be produced twice and none is missed.

questions.q: What changes if the input has duplicates?
questions.a: The `used`-by-position approach still works and naturally produces duplicate outputs, which you must then dedupe (e.g. insert into a set or skip equal values at the same depth). Skipping equal values at one level is the cheaper fix and is what problem 90 does.

questions.q: What is the complexity?
questions.a: $O(n \cdot n!)$ time -- there are n! leaves and copying each costs $O(n)$. Space is $O(n)$ for the recursion and the path, plus $O(n \cdot n!)$ for the output, which dominates everything.

problems.diagram:
n = 4 -> two solutions

  rows 0..3, one queen per row. Place in row i:
    cols   : set of occupied columns
    d1     : set of occupied (row - col)   diagonals
    d2     : set of occupied (row + col)   diagonals

  dfs(row):
    for c in range(n):
      if c in cols or (row-c) in d1 or (row+c) in d2:
        continue
      place, recurse, unplace

  trace row 0: c=0 ok -> row 1: c=0 taken, c=1 diag? row-c=0 ->
    d1 has 0 -> skip; c=2 row-c=-1 d1? no, row+c=3 d2? no
    -> place at (1,2) -> row 2: c=1 -> row 3: c=3 ->
    SOLUTION [[0,2],[1,4?]]... emits board 0 0 0 0 / 0 1 0 1

  the three conflict tests are exhaustive because a queen
  attacks along a row (impossible, one per row), a column,
  and two diagonals. Sets make each test O(1).
problems.cpp_vs_py: Backtracking is dominated by the cost of copying the current path at each node. Python's `path + ch` allocates and copies at every node, giving $O(n \cdot 	ext{output})$ where $O(	ext{output})$ suffices; mutating one list with append and pop fixes that. C++ has exactly the same trap with `std::string`, and the same fix with `push_back` and `pop_back`.
cpp_alts: `bitset<n>` per row and diagonal-gather operations make the conflict test a single mask AND -- the fastest known formulation.
Keeping `board[r] = c` per row makes emitting the board trivial; `vector<int> queen(n)` is simpler.
py_alts: Three Python `set`s give O(1) tests; three bitmasks on integers are faster in CPython because small-int bit ops are single operations.
Precomputing all diagonal indices avoids recomputing `row - c` and `row + c` at every node.
problems.trap: Using only the column check and forgetting one of the diagonals, or using absolute differences instead of the difference and sum. Absolute difference alone catches one diagonal family and misses the other.
problems.invariant: After placing queens in rows 0..row-1, the three sets contain exactly the columns, the row-minus-column values, and the row-plus-column values of the placed queens. Therefore the membership tests are exactly the three attack directions, and any candidate passing all three is conflict-free.

questions.q: Why is one queen per row guaranteed by the algorithm?
questions.a: Because the search places exactly one queen per row by construction -- it recurses row by row. A valid solution can also be rotated, so the first row always has a queen; that is why only row-wise placement is complete.

questions.q: What is the pruning power of the set tests?
questions.a: They cut the n! search to roughly $O(n! / n^{n/2})$ explored nodes for large n, because each new queen eliminates a growing fraction of the remaining columns. That is what makes n = 9 tractable while a naive row-column scan is not.

questions.q: How would bitsets improve this?
questions.a: Represent occupied columns, diagonals, and anti-diagonals as bitmasks; the test becomes three AND operations on machine words. For n up to 32 that is a handful of instructions versus three hash lookups, and it also makes the horizontal reflection symmetry cheap to exploit.

problems.one_liner: Every node of the tree is a subset, so emit as you go.
problems.core_objective: Return all subsets of a set of distinct integers, in any order.
problems.bounds: 0 <= nums.length <= 10, so at most 1024 subsets. An empty input yields one subset, the empty set.

approaches.name: · Backtracking include/exclude (best)
approaches.aha: dfs(i): i == n → record. Else dfs(i+1) (exclude) and dfs(i+1) with nums[i] appended (include).
approaches.py:
out, cur = [], []
    if i == len(nums):
        out.append(cur[:])
        return
    dfs(i + 1)
    cur.append(nums[i])
    dfs(i + 1)
    cur.pop()
approaches.why: Follows directly from the traversal count: ? time, ? space.

approaches.name: · Bitmask enumeration
approaches.aha: mask in 0..2^n-1: pick nums[j] iff bit j set. --------------------------------------------------------------------- DEEP DIVE · What "backtracking" literally does here The append/pop pair is the backtrack: append explores the include-branch, pop restores the shared list so the exclude sibling starts from an identical prefix. Total leaves 2^n, each copied once → O(n·2^n). --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(n · 2^n) MEMORY COMPLEXITY: O(n) recursion depth. =====================================================================
approaches.py:
out = []
for mask in range(1 << len(nums)):
    out.append([nums[j] for j in range(len(nums)) if mask & (1 << j)])
return out
approaches.why: constant passes over the bits of the value; hence the stated bounds.

problems.diagram:
nums = [1,2,3]   -> 8 subsets

  path=[]        EMIT []
   path=[1]      EMIT [1]
    path=[1,2]   EMIT [1,2]
     path=[1,2,3] EMIT [1,2,3]
    path=[1,3]   EMIT [1,3]
   path=[2]      EMIT [2]
    path=[2,3]   EMIT [2,3]
  path=[3]        EMIT [3]

  2^3 = 8 emissions, matching the node count of a binary tree
  of depth 3 (1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 nodes, 8 leaves) -- here
  every NODE is a solution, so 8 of the 15 nodes emit.

  include/exclude formulation:
   dfs(i, cur):
     if i == n: emit(cur); return
     dfs(i+1, cur)            # exclude nums[i]
     dfs(i+1, cur + [nums[i]]) # include nums[i]

  BITMASK alternative: for m in 0..2^n-1, bit j of m says
   whether nums[j] is in subset m -- no recursion at all.
problems.cpp_vs_py:
The append/pop pair is the backtrack: append explores the include-branch, pop restores the shared list so the exclude sibling starts from an identical prefix. Total leaves 2^n, each copied once → O(n·2^n). --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(n · 2^n)

=====================================================================
cpp_alts: The bitmask loop `for (int m = 0; m < (1<<n); ++m)` is branch-free and trivially correct for n <= 20.
Reserving the result to `1 << n` avoids repeated reallocation.
py_alts: `[list(c) for r in range(n+1) for c in combinations(nums, r)]` is C-level and gives all subsets sorted by size.
`itertools.chain.from_iterable` over `combinations(nums, r)` avoids materialising intermediate lists.
problems.trap: Emitting only at the leaves. That gives the subsets in a different form and, if the recursion is include/exclude, only emits at depth n -- losing every smaller subset unless the branch is handled separately.
problems.invariant: `path` is always a subset of nums containing only indices greater than the current recursion depth, so no index is used twice. Every subset is generated exactly once because each subset has a unique include/exclude signature, which corresponds to a unique root-to-node path.

questions.q: Why does the count match 2^n?
questions.a: Each of the n elements independently is either in or out, giving $2^n$ combinations. The recursion explores exactly that decision tree, emitting once per complete signature, so the count is right by construction rather than by filtering.

questions.q: When is the bitmask version preferable?
questions.a: When n is small (say <= 20) and you want no recursion at all: iterate m from 0 to $2^n - 1$ and read bit j to decide membership. It is branch-free and impossible to get wrong, at the cost of an $O(2^n)$ shift per element.

questions.q: How does this relate to permutation problems?
questions.a: Subsets are the include/exclude case (2 branches per level) whereas permutations are the pick-any-unused case (n branches). That difference in branching factor is why subsets have $2^n$ nodes and permutations $n!$, and it is the structural insight the category is built on.

    if not (0 <= i < m and 0 <= j < n) or vis[i][j] or board[i][j] != word[k]:
    vis[i][j] = True
    found = (dfs(i + 1, j, k + 1) or dfs(i - 1, j, k + 1) or
             dfs(i, j + 1, k + 1) or dfs(i, j - 1, k + 1))
    vis[i][j] = False
approaches.why: Follows directly from the traversal count: O(m·n·3^L) worst. time, O(L) recursion depth. space.

problems.diagram:
board = ["ABE","SFCS","ADEE"]  word = "ABCCED"

  dfs(r, c, k):   k = index into the word
    if out of bounds or board[r][c] != word[k]: return False
    if k == len(word) - 1: return True          # last char matched
    tmp = board[r][c]; board[r][c] = '#'        # MARK
    found = (dfs(r+1,c,k+1) or dfs(r-1,c,k+1)
             or dfs(r,c+1,k+1) or dfs(r,c-1,k+1))
    board[r][c] = tmp                          # UNMARK  <- load bearing
    return found

  why mark: without it, 'AAA' can walk a straight line forever
  by stepping back onto the previous cell.
  why unmark: a sibling branch needs the ORIGINAL character;
  leaving '#' makes the whole search fail.
problems.cpp_vs_py:
'\0' can never match an input letter, so "used" is encoded in the board itself — no allocation, no restore on the success path (early return unwinds without restoring, which is safe because we already found the answer). Worst case (all cells match the first char): O(m·n·3^L). --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(m·n·3^L) worst.

=====================================================================
cpp_alts: Mark with a sentinel character such as '\0' rather than '#' to be collision-proof against board contents.
A `used` bool grid costs $O(RC)$ extra space but avoids mutating the input, which matters if the caller reuses it.
py_alts: Passing the four neighbours as a literal tuple of (dr, dc) offsets avoids four near-duplicate recursive calls.
A `used` 2-D list is clean but allocates; in-place marking with restore is faster and is what the problem's mutation tolerance invites.
problems.trap: Forgetting to restore the cell after the recursive call. Every later path that needs that cell sees '#' and fails, so the answer is wrong even though the code looks symmetric at a glance.
problems.invariant: On entry to `dfs(r, c, k)`, the cells holding word[0..k-1] along the current path are all marked '#', so no unmark check is needed inside the recursion -- the marks themselves enforce the no-revisit rule. Restoring on the way out re-establishes the invariant for sibling branches.

questions.q: What is the time complexity, and why is it not simply O(RC * L)?
questions.a: A loose bound is $O(RC \cdot 4^L)$ from the branching, but the marking prunes hard: each path visits distinct cells, so the search is bounded by the number of simple paths, which is $O(3^L)$ per start because the previous cell is already marked and cannot be re-entered.

questions.q: Why is in-place marking better than a visited array here?
questions.a: It uses O(1) extra space and one array write instead of a bounds-checked 2-D lookup. The cost is that you must restore, which is one extra write per node -- a good trade at these sizes.

questions.q: When would a Trie be the right structure?
questions.a: When you must find ALL words in a large dictionary, not test a few. Then you share the walk across words instead of restarting from each cell per word, which is exactly problem 212.

problems.one_liner: Sort, then skip equal values at the same recursion level.
problems.core_objective: Return all unique subsets of a collection that may contain duplicates.
problems.bounds: 1 <= nums.length <= 10 so at most 1024 raw subsets; uniqueness must be enforced, not filtered afterwards.

approaches.name: · Backtracking with skip-duplicates (best)
approaches.aha: dfs(i) records cur, then for j in i..n: skip j if c[j]==c[j-1] (j>i), append c[j], recurse(j+1), pop.
approaches.py:
nums.sort()
out, cur = [], []
    out.append(cur[:])
    for j in range(i, len(nums)):
        if j > i and nums[j] == nums[j - 1]:
            continue
        cur.append(nums[j])
        dfs(j + 1)
approaches.why: Follows directly from the traversal count: ? time, ? space.

approaches.name: · Set of sorted tuples
approaches.aha: Generate every subset via bitmask, sort tuples, dedupe with a set. --------------------------------------------------------------------- DEEP DIVE · Why skipping the SECOND copy is enough Two duplicate values v produce identical subtrees only when used at the SAME level; the first v's subtree already contains every subset using v (any number of later copies). Skipping equal neighbors after a choice kills exactly the redundant subtrees — nothing is lost. --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(2^n) worst case (all distinct). MEMORY COMPLEXITY: O(n). =====================================================================
approaches.py:
nums.sort()
seen = set()
for mask in range(1 << len(nums)):
    cur = tuple(nums[j] for j in range(len(nums)) if mask & (1 << j))
    seen.add(cur)
return [list(t) for t in seen]
approaches.why: each element is probed once; pairs cancel or are recorded; hence the stated bounds.

problems.diagram:
nums = [1,2,2]
  raw subsets: 8  -> unique: 4

  sorted: [1,2,2]
  dfs(start=0, cur=[]):
    EMIT []
    i=0 c=1 -> dfs(1,[1])
      i=1 c=2 -> dfs(2,[1,2])
        i=2 c=2 -> dfs(3,[1,2,2]) EMIT [1,2,2]
      i=2 i>0 and c[2]==c[1] -> SKIP   <- avoids [1,2,2] twice
    i=1 c=2 -> dfs(2,[2])
      i=2 i>0 and c[2]==c[1] -> SKIP   <- avoids [2,2] from
                                          starting at index 1
    i=2 i>0 and c[2]==c[1] -> SKIP

  the rule: at a given recursion level, once you have taken
  c[i], you may not also take c[i+1] if they are equal. Taking
  the LATER equal element instead gives a canonical choice.
problems.cpp_vs_py:
Two duplicate values v produce identical subtrees only when used at the SAME level; the first v's subtree already contains every subset using v (any number of later copies). Skipping equal neighbors after a choice kills exactly the redundant subtrees — nothing is lost. --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(2^n) worst case (all distinct).

=====================================================================
cpp_alts: Sort then the same skip; `sort` plus `unique` on the input would lose multiplicity and is wrong.
`vector<bool> used(100)` as an alternative dedupe via set insertion works but costs a hash per leaf.
py_alts: `set(map(tuple, ...))` at the end dedupes but is $O(2^n \cdot n)$ and loses order.
The skip rule is strictly better: it avoids generating the duplicates at all.
problems.trap: Deduplicating the INPUT with `set(nums)`. That loses multiplicity, so `[1,2,2]` becomes `[1,2]` and the answer misses `[1,2,2]` entirely.
problems.invariant: With the array sorted, the skip `i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1]` ensures that within each recursion level, equal values are offered only at their first occurrence. Every distinct multiset therefore has exactly one index sequence, so no duplicate subset is generated and none is lost.

questions.q: Why `i > start` rather than `i > 0`?
questions.a: Because the skip should apply only among siblings at the same level. Using `i > 0` would also forbid legitimately choosing a second equal element deeper in the recursion, which is required for subsets like [1,2,2]. `start` marks where the current level began.

questions.q: Why does the skip work only on sorted input?
questions.a: It compares adjacent elements, so equal values must be adjacent. Sorting guarantees adjacency and is therefore a correctness precondition, not merely a speedup.

questions.q: What is the worst-case number of generated subsets?
questions.a: Exactly the number of distinct subsets, which is at most $2^n$ and equals $\prod_i (c_i + 1)$ for value multiplicities $c_i$. With the skip in place you generate each exactly once, so there is no wasted work.

problems.one_liner: Precompute the palindrome table, then DFS over cuts.
problems.core_objective: Return all partitions of a string such that every part is a palindrome.
problems.bounds: 1 <= s.length <= 2000 with lowercase letters, so the answer can be up to $2^{n-1}$ -- output-bound. A palindrome table is $O(n^2)$ time and space.

approaches.name: · DFS + direct palindrome probe (best for short input)
approaches.aha: dfs(start): start == n → record. For end in start..n: if the slice is a palindrome, take it, recurse(end+1).
approaches.why: every node is visited once and returns O(1) state; hence the stated bounds.

approaches.name: · Precomputed palindrome table
approaches.aha: isPal[i][j] via DP in O(n²), then O(1) queries in the same DFS. --------------------------------------------------------------------- DEEP DIVE · Table vs probe trade-off The probe costs O(n) per cut probe — fine for small strings, but a 2^n-shaped search tree makes the table worthwhile past n ≈ 20. DP identity: s[i]==s[j] and (j-i < 2 or isPal[i+1][j-1]). --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : A1 O(n·2^n) worst; A2 O(2^n) + O(n²) build. MEMORY COMPLEXITY: O(n²) for the table in A2. =====================================================================
approaches.time: A1 O(n·2^n) worst; A2 O(2^n) + O(n²) build.
approaches.space: O(n²) for the table in A2.
approaches.why: Follows directly from the traversal count: A1 O(n·2^n) worst; A2 O(2^n) + O(n²) build. time, O(n²) for the table in A2. space.

problems.diagram:
s = "aab"  -> [["a","a","b"], ["aa","b"]]

  isPal[i][j] = s[i]==s[j] and (j-i<2 or isPal[i+1][j-1])

   a  a  b
  a T  F  F
  a .  T  F
  b .  .  T

  dfs(start):
    if start == n: emit(path); return
    for end in range(start, n):
      if isPal[start][end]:
        path.push(s[start..end])
        dfs(end+1)
        path.pop()

   start=0: end=0 'a' pal -> dfs(1)
        start=1: end=1 'a' pal -> dfs(2)
              end=2 'ab' not pal
              dfs(2): end=2 'b' pal -> dfs(3) EMIT [a,a,b]
        end=2 'aab' not pal
   start=0: end=1 'aa' pal -> dfs(2)
        end=2 'b' pal -> dfs(3) EMIT [aa,b]

  O(n^2) table beats testing each candidate substring inline,
  which is O(n^3) in total.
problems.cpp_vs_py:
The probe costs O(n) per cut probe — fine for small strings, but a 2^n-shaped search tree makes the table worthwhile past n ≈ 20. DP identity: s[i]==s[j] and (j-i < 2 or isPal[i+1][j-1]). --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : A1 O(n·2^n) worst; A2 O(2^n) + O(n²) build.

=====================================================================
cpp_alts: A `vector<vector<bool>>` table is compact; a 2-D char array is faster.
Fill the table by increasing substring length so the recurrence's dependency is already computed.
py_alts: A list-of-lists of bools beats a dict of tuples.
For n = 2000 the table is 4e6 entries -- Python lists of bools cost ~32 MB, so a bytearray per row is leaner.
problems.trap: Testing palindromes by reversing each candidate substring inline. That is $O(n^3)$ overall and will not pass at n = 2000.
problems.invariant: `isPal[i][j]` is true iff s[i..j] is a palindrome, established by the recurrence for j-i < 2 and the inner interval otherwise. Therefore `dfs(start)` explores exactly the partitions whose first part starts at `start` and whose remaining parts partition the suffix, so every valid partition appears exactly once.

questions.q: Why precompute the palindrome table?
questions.a: Because the same substring is tested repeatedly across different partitions. Precomputing makes each test O(1), giving $O(n^2)$ for the table and $O(2^n)$ for the enumeration (output-bound). Inline testing repeats work and pushes the total to $O(n^3)$.

questions.q: What is the actual complexity?
questions.a: $O(n^2)$ for the table plus the number of partial partitions explored, which is bounded by the output size. The theoretical worst case is $O(n \cdot 2^n)$ because there can be $2^{n-1}$ partitions.

questions.q: When is the problem output-bound rather than time-bound?
questions.a: When s is all the same character, e.g. "aaaa...", because then every substring is a palindrome and every set of cut positions yields a valid partition -- giving exactly $2^{n-1}$ outputs. Any algorithm must spend that much just to write them down.

problems.one_liner: Split on a bad character, or slide a window by distinct count.
problems.core_objective: Return the length of the longest substring in which every character appears at least k times.
problems.bounds: 1 <= s.length <= 1e4, k >= 1, and lowercase letters only. If no valid substring exists the answer is 0, which is the common failure output.

approaches.name: · Divide & conquer on blocker chars (best)
approaches.aha: Count in s; all counts ≥ k → whole string valid. Else split at each blocker and take the max over pieces.
approaches.why: the recursion splits the work; the bound is the sum over levels; hence the stated bounds.

approaches.name: · Sliding window per distinct-count
approaches.aha: For c in 1..26: longest window with ≤ c distinct letters where every letter occurs ≥ k times — the O(26n) two-pointer classic. --------------------------------------------------------------------- DEEP DIVE · Why splitting on blockers is exact If 'x' occurs 2 < k times, any valid substring excludes x and lies entirely within one gap between x's. Gaps are independent, so recursion over gaps is complete and correct. A2's twist: "every char ≥ k" alone isn't a monotone window predicate, but fixing the distinct count IS — hence the 26 sweeps. --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : A1 O(n²) worst; A2 O(26n). MEMORY COMPLEXITY: O(n) / O(1) counters. =====================================================================
approaches.why: Follows directly from the traversal count: A1 O(n²) worst; A2 O(26n). time, O(n) / O(1) counters. space.

problems.diagram:
s = "aaabbcccc", k = 3  -> answer 10? check:
   'aaa' a:3 ok  'bb'  b:2 < 3  -> b is a BLOCKER
   'cccc' c:4 ok  a:3 ok
   whole string: a4 b2 c4 -> b < 3 -> invalid
   split at b: "aaa" (3) and "cccc" (4) -> max 4
   ANSWER 4

  DIVIDE AND CONQUER:
   if already valid(s): return len(s)      -- shortcut
   find the leftmost bad char c
   left  = recurse(s[:i])
   right = recurse(s[i+1:])
   return max(left, right)

  SLIDING WINDOW variant:
   track `distinct` (count of chars with count >= k)
   shrink while distinct > target for target in 1..26
   the answer is the max over all targets
problems.cpp_vs_py:
If 'x' occurs 2 < k times, any valid substring excludes x and lies entirely within one gap between x's. Gaps are independent, so recursion over gaps is complete and correct. A2's twist: "every char ≥ k" alone isn't a monotone window predicate, but fixing the distinct count IS — hence the 26 sweeps. --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : A1 O(n²) worst; A2 O(26n).

=====================================================================
cpp_alts: Frequency arrays indexed by char avoid any hashing in both the split and the window version.
The divide and conquer can use `string::find_first_of` for the split points, but an explicit scan is clearer.
py_alts: `Counter` or a 26-list for frequencies; a list is faster in CPython.
Iterating `target` from 1 to 26 with a reused window avoids re-implementing divide and conquer entirely.
problems.trap: Assuming the whole string is valid, or forgetting the early `if valid(s): return len(s)` shortcut which the divide-and-conquer needs to avoid infinite splitting.
problems.invariant: In the window variant, for a fixed `target`, the window is shrunk until at most `target` characters appear at least k times. Adding a character can only increase that count and removing one can only decrease it, so the shrink loop is monotone and each pointer advances at most n times, giving $O(n)$ per target and $O(26n)$ overall.

questions.q: Why does the divide and conquer need the validity shortcut?
questions.a: Because if the string is valid we must return its full length rather than split. Without the check, a fully valid string still gets split at its first bad character -- and there is none, so the code would either index out of range or recurse forever.

questions.q: What is the complexity of the sliding window variant?
questions.a: $O(\sigma n)$ where sigma is the alphabet size (26), since you try each target count of qualifying characters. That is linear for a fixed alphabet and avoids recursion entirely, which is why it is often the better interview answer.

questions.q: Why is splitting on a bad character correct?
questions.a: A character with fewer than k occurrences in the current string has fewer than k in any substring containing it, so no valid substring can include that position. Every valid substring therefore lies entirely to the left or entirely to the right of it, so the two sides can be solved independently.
